Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Rabbi Benjamin, a 63-year-old North American man, came to therapy after a long history of trauma that began decades ago when he was forced to flee his homeland as a refugee. The traumatic experience left deep scars that have persisted into his current life and work. Benjamin recounts the harrowing journey of escaping violence, where sudden touches from people in chaotic crowds often led to physical confrontations. This fear has translated into an intense aversion to unexpected touch today, which is particularly challenging given his role as a community leader where people often reach out for support or comfort unexpectedly. The memory of weapons and shouting during those turbulent days also remains vivid; these triggers are reactivated whenever he sees similar objects or hears loud voices in the synagogue or community center. Since then, Benjamin has employed various maladaptive strategies to cope with his overwhelming distress. When confronted by a trigger, such as an unexpected touch or seeing a weapon-like object, he often tells himself that he deserves this suffering because of what happened back then, believing that he must atone for not being able to prevent the violence. This punishment thinking has also led him to engage in distraction techniques, where he immerses himself in work or other activities to avoid confronting his painful memories. The negative appraisals that Benjamin holds about himself and others have significantly impacted his ability to feel safe and secure. He believes that his body is constantly on high alert, reacting as if the danger from his past still lurks around every corner. This sense of being in constant peril has made it difficult for him to concentrate on daily tasks, such as leading services or counseling community members. Benjamin's feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy have only intensified his fear. He often thinks that he cannot rely on himself to protect himself from future harm and believes that someone else could have prevented the traumatic events from happening. These thoughts have led him to engage in safe-seeking behaviors, such as always choosing a seat where he can see all entrances or staying within a very limited set of familiar places where he feels protected. The interplay between his triggers and maladaptive strategies is evident in how quickly these mechanisms kick into gear when he encounters something that reminds him of the past. For instance, if he hears shouting during a heated debate in the synagogue, he immediately starts to distract himself by focusing on administrative tasks or telling himself that he deserves this discomfort as part of his penance. Benjamin's negative appraisals have also created a feedback loop where they perpetuate both his threat perceptions and his triggers. His belief that his body is an enemy constantly reacting in danger mode has led him to feel anxious even in safe environments, further reinforcing his sense of vulnerability. Additionally, the notion that he cannot rely on himself has made it challenging for him to trust others emotionally, leading him to avoid intimacy and emotional closeness with both his partner and congregants. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have had significant consequences on Benjamin’s personal and professional life. His work as a rabbi requires him to be present and engaged with the community, but his concentration difficulties and avoidance behaviors have led to missed opportunities for deep connections and support within the synagogue. He has become increasingly isolated, both personally and professionally. What finally brought Benjamin to seek help was a series of recent incidents where his maladaptive coping mechanisms failed him, leaving him feeling even more vulnerable and distressed. His partner had noticed his increasing withdrawal and urged him to find professional support. Although he is afraid that therapy might bring up too many painful memories, he hopes for a way to regain control over his life and feel safe again within the community he has dedicated himself to serve. In summary, Benjamin's traumatic history has left deep psychological scars that manifest through specific triggers, maladaptive coping strategies, persistent threat perceptions, and negative appraisals. His belief in his own inadequacy and fear of re-experiencing past trauma have led him to a cycle of heightened anxiety, avoidance behaviors, and self-doubt. Seeking therapy now represents both a moment of vulnerability and hope for Benjamin as he grapples with the long-lasting effects of his traumatic experiences.
